source.title: Prefrontal cortex projections to the nucleus reuniens suppress freezing following two-way signaled avoidance training

confidence_rationale: Directly supports the claim's central architectural bet (a ventromedial-PFC-sourced projection suppresses freezing specifically as a consequence of avoidance being learned, not tonically) with three convergent chemogenetic/pharmacological experiments. Confidence held below 0.7 because the projection target (nucleus reuniens, a thalamic relay) has no REE analogue and the paper does not directly measure the suppression signal's magnitude growing WITH training -- it infers training-dependence from a post-training-only test design plus cited prior work, rather than from a within-subject trajectory.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In rats given two-way signaled active avoidance (SAA) training followed by an off-baseline test 24h later (10 CS presentations in a novel context, avoidance impossible), inactivating ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) -- either generally (DREADDs), via its terminals specifically in the nucleus reuniens (NR), or by directly inactivating NR itself -- increased CS-evoked freezing in previously successful avoiders back up toward the level of animals that never learned to avoid. All three manipulations converged: general vmPFC inactivation (p<0.001), vmPFC->NR terminal inactivation (p<0.01), and NR inactivation alone (p<0.01) each disinhibited freezing. The author frames this vmPFC->NR pathway as 'a common pathway recruited by memory phenomena that suppress freezing' rather than a constitutively active brake, drawing on prior extinction-literature findings that the same circuit's suppressive role only appears after substantial training.
mapping.ree_translation: This is the clearest LEARNING-DEPENDENT counterpart to the Ho et al. (2025) IL-PV finding in this same literature_type. Where Ho et al. found an infralimbic freeze-suppression signal that appears almost immediately and does not scale with training, Moscarello's data are consistent with a ventromedial-PFC-sourced suppression that is specifically a consequence of avoidance having been ACQUIRED -- disabling the pathway in already-successful avoiders makes them behave like animals that never learned, i.e. the suppression is doing work that tracks learned competence rather than being present from the outset. This is the shape of evidence MECH-357's falsifiable prediction needs (suppression scaling with LEARNED efficacy), even though it comes via a different downstream target (nucleus reuniens, a midline thalamic relay to hippocampus, not the amygdala/PAG pathway MECH-357 wires the gate through) and via a coarser test (a single post-training snapshot, not a continuous within-subject learning curve).
mapping.mapping_caveat: The projection is vmPFC to nucleus reuniens, a thalamic relay implicated in memory retrieval and cortico-hippocampal communication -- not the direct suppression of PAG/CeA output that MECH-357 wires the ilPFC-analog gate through. So this paper supports the higher-level claim (vmPFC-region suppression of freezing is contingent on learned avoidance competence) without confirming the specific circuit MECH-357 models. The paper also does not directly track the suppression signal's magnitude across acquisition trials -- the training-dependence argument rests partly on the post-training-only design (naive comparison groups) and partly on citation of separate extinction studies, which is weaker than a within-subject trajectory would be.
mapping.source_context: Adult male rats; three daily sessions of two-way signaled active avoidance (shuttle box, tone CS, footshock US); chemogenetic (hM4Di-CNO) and pharmacological (muscimol) inactivation of vmPFC, vmPFC terminals in NR, and NR itself; off-baseline freezing test 24h post-training.

confidence_components.notes: mapping_fidelity held moderate because the anatomical route (NR, a thalamic relay) diverges from MECH-357's amygdala/PAG-facing gate; transfer_risk reflects that training-dependence is argued rather than directly shown as a within-subject trajectory. Included specifically because it is the clearest available counterweight to the Ho et al. (2025) entry's learning-independence finding, and the tension between the two is itself the honest state of this literature.
